title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLIX
paragraphs:
“A task too strong for wizard spells
This squire had brought about;
’T is easy dropping stones in wells,
But who shall get them out?”
“I wish to God we could keep Dorothea from hearing about this,” said Sir James Chettam. His brow was slightly furrowed, and his mouth showed profound disgust.
He stood on the hearthrug in the library of Lowick Grange, talking to Mr. Brooke. Mr. Casaubon had been buried the previous day, and Dorothea was still too ill to leave her room.

“That would be difficult, Chettam, you know. She's an executor, and she likes looking into these matters—property, land, things of that sort. She has ideas of her own, you know,” said Mr. Brooke. He nervously put on his eyeglasses and examined the edges of a folded paper in his hand. “And she'll want to take part—you may be sure that as an executor Dorothea will insist on taking part. Besides, she turned twenty-one last December, you know. I can't prevent anything.”

Sir James stared silently at the carpet for a moment. Then he suddenly raised his eyes and fixed them on Mr. Brooke. “I'll tell you what we can do. We must keep all business away from Dorothea until she recovers, and the moment she can be moved, she must come to us. Being with Celia and the baby will be the very best thing for her, and help her pass the time. Meanwhile, you must get rid of Ladislaw: you must send him out of the country.” At this, the full intensity of his disgust returned to Sir James's face.
Putting his hands behind his back, Mr. Brooke walked to the window and gave himself a little shake to straighten up before answering.
“Easily said, Chettam. That's easily said, you know.”
“My dear sir,” Sir James insisted, keeping his indignation within the bounds of respect, “you brought him here, and you're keeping him here—through the work you give him, I mean.”

“Yes, but I can't suddenly dismiss him without giving reasons, my dear Chettam. Ladislaw has been invaluable, entirely satisfactory. I believe I've done this district a service by bringing him—by bringing him, you know.” Mr. Brooke turned round to finish with a nod.

“Then it's a pity this district couldn't have managed without him. That's all I can say. In any event, as Dorothea's brother-in-law, I believe I'm entitled to object strongly to her friends doing anything that keeps him here. You must admit I have a right to speak when my wife's sister's dignity is at stake?”
Sir James was growing heated.
“Certainly, my dear Chettam, certainly. But your ideas and mine are different—different—”

“Not about this thing Casaubon has done, I hope,” Sir James broke in. “I say he has compromised Dorothea most unfairly. Nothing could be meaner or less worthy of a gentleman than this—adding such a codicil to a will he made when he married, a will her family knew of and relied on. It's a direct insult to Dorothea!”

“Well, Casaubon was rather unreasonable about Ladislaw, you know. Ladislaw explained the reason to me—disliked the direction he'd taken, you know. Ladislaw didn't think much of Casaubon's theories, Thoth and Dagon—all that. And I fancy Casaubon resented the independent position Ladislaw had established. I saw their letters to one another, you know. Poor Casaubon was rather buried in his books—he knew nothing of the world.”

“Ladislaw may choose to present it that way,” said Sir James. “But I believe Casaubon was simply jealous of him because of Dorothea. People will assume she gave him some cause, and that's what makes it so abominable—linking her name with this young fellow's.”

“My dear Chettam, nothing will come of it, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, sitting down and putting on his eyeglass again. “It's entirely in keeping with Casaubon's odd ways. Take this paper, ‘Synoptical Tabulation’ and so forth, ‘for the use of Mrs. Casaubon.’ It was locked in the desk with the will. Presumably he wanted Dorothea to publish his research, eh? And she'll do it, you know. She's taken an extraordinary interest in his studies.”
“My dear sir,” said Sir James impatiently, “that has nothing to do with it. The question is whether you agree that young Ladislaw ought to be sent away.”

“Well, no—I don't see the urgency. Perhaps it will work itself out in time. As for gossip, sending him away won't stop that, you know. People say whatever they want to say, whether they have evidence for it or not,” said Mr. Brooke, growing perceptive about truths that supported his own wishes. “I could get rid of Ladislaw up to a point—take the ‘Pioneer’ away from him, that sort of thing. But I couldn't force him out of the country if he didn't want to go—didn't want to, you know.”
Mr. Brooke maintained his position as calmly as though they were merely discussing last year's weather, ending with his usual pleasant nod. It was an infuriating kind of obstinacy.

“Good God!” exclaimed Sir James, with all the passion he was capable of. “Let's find him a position; let's spend some money on him. He could join a colonial governor's staff! Grampus might take him—and I could write to Fulke about it.”

“But Ladislaw won't let himself be shipped off like livestock, my dear fellow. He has his own ideas. I believe that if he left me tomorrow, you'd only hear more about him in the district. With his gift for public speaking and drafting documents, few men could match him as an agitator—an agitator, you know.”
“Agitator!” Sir James repeated bitterly. He felt that pronouncing each syllable with the right emphasis was enough to expose how hateful the thing was.

“But let's be reasonable, Chettam. Now, Dorothea. As you say, she ought to go to Celia as soon as she can. She can stay in your house, and meanwhile matters may settle down quietly. Let's not rush to fire our guns, you know. Standish will keep this to himself, and the news will be old before anyone hears it. Twenty things might take Ladislaw away without any action on my part, you know.”
“So I must understand that you refuse to do anything?”
“Refuse, Chettam? No—I didn't say refuse. I simply can't see what I could do. Ladislaw is a gentleman.”
“I'm glad to hear it!” said Sir James, irritated enough to forget his manners a little. “Casaubon certainly wasn't.”
“Well, it would have been worse if he'd added a codicil preventing her from ever marrying again, you know.”
“I'm not so sure,” said Sir James. “That would have shown more delicacy.”
“Just one of poor Casaubon's eccentricities! That attack affected his brain a little. None of it matters. She doesn't _want_ to marry Ladislaw.”

“But the codicil is worded to make everyone believe she did. I believe nothing of the kind about Dorothea,” said Sir James. Then he frowned. “But I distrust Ladislaw. I'll say it plainly: I distrust Ladislaw.”

“I couldn't act immediately on those grounds, Chettam. Indeed, even if we could pack him off—send him to Norfolk Island, something of that sort—it would make Dorothea look worse to anyone who knew about it. It would suggest we didn't trust her—didn't trust her, you know.”
Mr. Brooke's discovery of an unanswerable argument did nothing to calm Sir James. He reached for his hat, signalling that he would argue no further, and said, still heatedly—
“Well, all I can say is that Dorothea has already been sacrificed once because her friends failed to take enough care. As her brother, I'll do everything I can to protect her now.”

“The best thing you can do is bring her to Freshitt as soon as possible, Chettam. I'm entirely in favour of that plan,” said Mr. Brooke, pleased to have won the argument. Parting with Ladislaw just then would have been extremely inconvenient. Parliament might be dissolved any day, and the voters needed persuading which course would best serve the country's interests. Mr. Brooke honestly believed those interests would be served by electing him to Parliament. He sincerely offered the powers of his mind to the nation.
